newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: JOBS-South Africa fights uphill battle on jobs.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-South Africa fights uphill battle on jobs.

text.p: Just as South Africa tries to heal its black-and-white divide, a new rift is widening which could be even more turbulent -- between those in jobs and those without.

President Nelson Mandela faces what looks like a Herculean task just to prevent things getting worse, let alone meet his goal of massive job creation to alleviate unemployment estimated at around 30 percent of a workforce of some 15 million.
"Unemployment is the single greatest threat to peace," Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said last year. "We must devise growth that creates jobs."
New jobs are outpaced by a third of a million school leavers a year and by illegal immigrants flooding into what has, since apartheid's defeat in 1994, become a mecca for Africa's poor.
They number up to four million, stoking the resentment of struggling South Africans.

In a country that doesn't know how big its population really is and has scant welfare, no one is sure exactly how many are out of work. But a worried Mandela has put jobs at the top of his economic policy goals.

"Social instability is already with us and is reflected in the high crime statistics. If you can't eat and you can't get welfare, you steal to survive," warned Jan de Jager, chief economist at the National Productivity Institute.

The search for jobs is driving people from rural areas where they were penned in under apartheid to the squatter camps that are mushrooming around Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban. ARE GOVERNMENT TARGETS TOO AMBITIOUS?

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals estimates a quarter of the estimated labour force is without work, with another 20 percent working outside the formal sector -- scratching out a living selling onions on a street corner or guarding cars.
Black women are hardest hit, with one in two out of work.
Mandela's African National Congress government is pinning hopes on its 10-month-old macroeconomic policy that aims to create 400,000 jobs a year by the turn of the century.

Last year's target was 126,000 jobs, but the news is not good. The central Reserve Bank said latest figures available, for the first half of 1996, showed a drop of more than five percent in seasonally adjusted non-agricultural employment.
Patchy economic progress since the dying days of white minority rule has brought growth, but without the jobs.

Foreign investment, returning after the end of sanctions and South Africa's political isolation, has so far centred on government bonds or shares of existing companies rather than building new factories.

"The recovery in overall economic activity since the middle of 1993 has not succeeded in improving the employment-creating potential of the South African economy," the Reserve Bank added in its last quarterly report.
"Average annual employment in the formal non-agricultural sectors of the economy increased only once in the past six years when it rose at a year-to-year rate of 0.7 percent in 1995."

Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, favourite to succeed Mandela when he steps down in 1999, said last month the economy was on the right track but spoke only of a slower loss of jobs, not of any work boom.
"Employment losses are tapering off," he said, "productivity is rising, unit labour costs are declining."

He said projected economic growth of 2.9 percent this year was too low to cut unemployment, but the government hopes to double this to six percent by 2000, a level which could start to make a difference. CHANGING FACE OF EMPLOYMENT
Tourism has been identified as the main job-creating hope as more traditional industries such as engineering flounder.

Mining, the foundation stone of South Africa's economy, has also shed jobs heavily, leaving contract workers from Lesotho, Mozambique and other neighbour states without work. It still provides 400,000 jobs and manufacturing remains the biggest employer, with 1.4 million jobs.
Officials do not like to talk about the consequences of failure among the masses who hoped that President Mandela and democracy would quickly transform their lives.

Three years into the new era, frustration among unemployed is not yet boiling over into political unrest, but analysts say friction between the idle and those in work who fiercely defend their pay and conditions is an added risk. LABOUR MARKET CRITICISED FOR RIGIDITY
The macro-economic plan commits the government to boosting training and, vaguely, to deregulating the labour market.

A draft Employment Standards Act recognises for the first time many kinds of employment that exist in practice, such as part-timers and "permanent casuals". It would also allow the more flexible working hours that employers demand.
But the powerful unions, though formally allied with the ruling ANC, are deeply suspicious that a more flexible job market is merely a ruse by big business to cut wages.
Employers complain labour is too rigid, unproductive and costly, a combination that puts off foreign investors and leaves South Africa way down the global competitiveness league.

"A country with such high unemployment can't afford above-inflation pay hikes like we have now," one executive said. "Lower wages would create more jobs. It's the best way to spread wealth around more fairly, and to generate new wealth."
Some South Africans, however, are not prepared to wait.
The scourge of violent crime is often blamed on the increasingly young, long-term unemployed who live in a country with one of the world's most unequal wealth distributions.
The most marked rise in crime last year involved petty theft, and top crime statistician Chris de Kock said the desperation of the unemployed was a root cause.
"This (petty theft) is by the person who steals because of need and not because of greed," he told a news conference.

Economist Elsabe Loots told a productivity conference last year that South Africa was saddled with 1.5 million "discouraged workers" -- the unskilled unemployed under 30 who had given up hope of finding work -- one of the highest rates in the world.
